content:
Security researchers have discovered a flaw in Apple's iCloud Private Relay service. While the feature is designed to protect users' real IP addresses, it may actually leak them to websites.

New iCloud Private Relay vulnerability

This iCloud Private Relay vulnerability was discovered by security researchers Tommy Mysk and Talal Haj Bakry, who detailed the issue on their website.

They said: "In short, any website that supports or pretends to support passkeys can see the user's real IP address, even if they have iCloud Private Relay turned on."

A refresher: iCloud Private Relay is not a VPN. As we've explained before, it only protects your IP address in Safari, while a VPN protects all your device's traffic at the system level.

According to 404 Media, the issue stems from a series of problems in Apple's WebKit engine and how it handles passkeys.

There's a quirk in how passkeys work — they're a widely secure, WebAuthn-based alternative to usernames and passwords — the user's device issues network requests outside the browser. In other words, that request basically bypasses Private Relay and exposes the user's real IP address, even though from the user's perspective, they may think they're just interacting with a website as usual. The researchers wrote in their report: "Because the assertion request is issued by the operating system's authentication service rather than by Safari, it never enters Private Relay's proxy path. Regardless, the destination server will see the device's real IP address."

On iOS, the situation is even more serious, because all browsers (in most countries) are required to use Apple's WebKit engine:

Mysk said they reported the issue to the Tor Project, which called the situation "very serious." However, the company reportedly did not provide a timeline for fixing the issue, but agreed to let Mysk publicly disclose it.

Mysk also submitted a security report to Apple, which currently shows that a fix is planned for fall 2026: "We plan to address the issue you reported."

You can check whether you're affected by this issue through a website set up by the researchers.

Today's report follows another vulnerability affecting Apple's "Hide My Email" feature. That flaw, which allowed anyone to access users' real email addresses, was fixed by Apple last month.
